| [NOTE-157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-157.md) v2 | Roberts — Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds | If a substantial class of mental states (interoceptive, affective, perceptual, and bodily-agentive states such as effort, trying and ownership) depends on an animate body, then today's disembodied chatbots lack them, and their many self-ascriptions of such states are "systematically untrue". Roberts argues that users can nonetheless engage chatbots through make-believe, as a new kind of fictional character that is interactive, co-constructed, self-involving and blended with the real world. He argues that this fictionalist stance escapes the epistemic norms that bind realist belief. | Read |
| [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md) v4 | Clark & Chalmers — The Extended Mind | The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. Otto's notebook entry is its example of such a standing belief. From this it infers, in one paragraph, that the self extends too. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. The paper explicitly says they are not necessary and sufficient conditions. | Read |
| [NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md) | Bechara, Damasio, Tranel & Damasio — Deciding advantageously before knowing the advantageous strategy | Ten controls and six ventromedial prefrontal patients play the four-deck gambling task while anticipatory skin-conductance responses (SCRs) and verbal reports are tracked. Every control and no patient develops anticipatory SCRs; three patients who can state the right strategy still choose badly. Controls prefer the good decks significantly only from the hunch period, and the pre-hunch SCR effect is a group-by-period interaction, not a deck difference, so "before knowing" is better supported for articulated strategy than for any awareness at all. | Read |
| [NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md) | Damasio — The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | The somatic marker hypothesis as its author stated it in 1996. Ventromedial prefrontal cortex stores links between classes of situation and the body states that accompanied them; on recurrence it re-enacts those states, via the body or an "as if" loop, and the re-enacted state marks imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, pruning the space reasoning must search. The evidence is summarised from earlier lesion and skin-conductance studies, without numbers. The mechanism is argued, not shown, and the paper says it is not a theory of prefrontal cortex as a whole. | Read |
| [NOTE-343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-343.md) | Rupert — Challenges to the Hypothesis of Extended Cognition | Rupert separates extended cognition (HEC) from embedded cognition (HEMC) and from content externalism, then argues that HEC loses to HEMC on conservatism. [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s criteria give a dilemma: without past endorsement they overgenerate beliefs; with it the organism is privileged. Memory research (conversation, negative transfer, the generation effect, power laws) shows external stores are a different kind, and a generic kind spanning both does no explanatory work. | Read |
| [NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md) | Intelligence without representation | A methodological manifesto with working robots behind it. Brooks argues that AI should build complete autonomous Creatures incrementally and test them in the real world, and that intelligence should be decomposed into parallel activity-producing layers, each running from sensing to action, not into perception, central reasoning and action. His robots have no central representation or control, and their coherence exists "in the eye of an observer", as in Minsky's account of human behaviour. The evidence is three layers on one robot, described, not measured, and the broad hypothesis about representation is flagged as a hypothesis. | Read |
| [NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md) | Chalmers — Extended Cognition and Extended Consciousness | Chalmers restates the 1998 extended-mind thesis as a claim about constitution through sensorimotor interaction, because the original statement is satisfied by wired-in "extended circuits" that the critics accept. He keeps the perception-action boundary as the strongest objection, and argues that consciousness does not extend because it needs information directly available for global control, and perception makes availability indirect. Both moves are proposed and defended against a few cases, not demonstrated. | Read |
| [NOTE-363](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-363.md) | Clark — Intrinsic content, active memory and the extended mind | Clark defends [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) against Adams and Aizawa's intrinsic-content objection: the notion is unclear, silicon could carry it, and their own concession that not every cognitive state needs non-derived content lets a conventional encoding serve as a belief's vehicle. Against the active-memory objection, he concedes the notebook is static and argues that how and when memory is updated is a difference below the level that matters. He closes on brains as open-ended controllers and persons as forensic, not biological, items. | Read |
| [NOTE-368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-368.md) | Adams & Aizawa — The bounds of cognition | Adams and Aizawa grant [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s parity sentence but deny that any actual case meets it. Cognition, they assume, needs non-derived content and a distinctive kind of causal process. Otto's inscriptions have only derived content, Otto's retrieval uses vision and motor control that Inga's does not, and coupling a process to its surroundings does not extend it. So cognition is brain-bound as a contingent fact, and human-plus-tool systems are too motley for a science. | Read |
| [NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md) | Chalmers — Foreword to Supersizing the Mind | Ten years after [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md), its co-author says the iPhone has made the thesis vivid, that the only principled objection is the perception-action boundary, and that the right reply is to let belief-ascription follow explanatory purpose, so that Otto's belief is extended for some explanations and not others. Consciousness probably stays internal, because no twin case for it can be built. The thesis needs only a weak parity-style functionalism. | Read |
| [NOTE-380](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-380.md) | Adams & Aizawa — Defending the Bounds of Cognition | A reply to a manuscript of Clark's "Memento's Revenge". It names the coupling-constitution fallacy, coupled is not part of, and restates the 2001 marks of the cognitive. Against Clark's Euler-circle case it separates how a diagram gets its meaning from how a mental image of it does. Against a "brain-tool science" it argues that tools are an open-ended motley. The fallacy is shown by one analogy, and the processing differences are asserted, not measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | An enactive account of social cognition built on coordination dynamics. When coordination and the encounter shape each other, the interaction gains its own precarious operational closure; it is social only if the interactors stay autonomous. Coordinated sense-making then ranges from one partner's sense-making being modulated to meanings made jointly. Conceptual throughout; evidence is illustrative (corridor, charades, mother–infant timing, perceptual crossing). | Read |
| [NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Minimal agency needs a self-individuated system that is the source of modulations of its coupling with the environment and regulates them by norms it generates. An autonomous organization, a precarious network of mutually enabling processes, generates all three when it adaptively modulates its coupling for its own maintenance. | [NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso's retrospective on HKB. The relative-phase equation dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ has stable in-phase and anti-phase states for b/a > 1/4 and only in-phase below; with noise the switch is a nonequilibrium phase transition with critical fluctuations and slowing. Symmetry breaking gives metastability (relative coordination); merged with Kuramoto it models groups. The same dynamics is reported within and between people and in brain activity. A first-person account, not a review. | Read |
| [NOTE-719](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-719.md) v2 | Di Paolo — Autopoiesis, Adaptivity, Teleology, Agency | Autopoiesis, read as conservation, gives only an all-or-nothing norm that an observer can see and the system cannot use. | [NOTE-720](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-720.md) v2 | Weber & Varela — Life after Kant | An argument, not a model: Kant's natural purposes (§§ 64–65), Jonas's metabolism and Maturana and Varela's autopoiesis converge on an intrinsic teleology, in which a self-producing system's maintenance of its own identity is its purpose and the source of value for it. The boundary is in the definition (components "constitute the system as a distinguishable unity"), but no test tells a produced boundary from an imposed one, and a multicellular organism is said not to be autopoietic itself. | [NOTE-727](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-727.md) | Rubin, Roli, Stano & Damiano — Genealogies of organizational closure | A conceptual genealogy of the notions of closure (closure to information, cyclic, operational, semantic, catalytic, metabolic, closure to efficient causation, closure of constraints) from mathematical logic, cybernetics, systems theory, thermodynamics, relational biology and the biology of cognition. Its thesis is that closure is best read as a circular organization of efficient causes by which a living system produces the conditions of its own existence. That is not feedback, self-organization or a catalytic cycle, and it cannot be exhaustively characterized as a state-determined syntactic procedure. Current AI, agentic LLM systems included, is said to approximate closure without instantiating it. The genealogy is historical; the non-computability and AI verdicts are asserted or argued from Rosen, not demonstrated. | Read |
| [NOTE-826](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-826.md) | Turvey — Preliminaries to a theory of action | An essay, not a study. The executive cannot command muscles one by one, so acts are built from relatively autonomous coordinative structures, reflexes and their functional combinations, a term Turvey takes from Easton (1972). Higher levels specify equivalence classes of acceptable states and tune the parameters of these units, like the stiffness and rest length of a spring. The spinal cord is shown, by reflex probes, to be retuned before a voluntary movement, and optical information may set the tuning directly. | Read |
| [NOTE-867](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-867.md) | Hutchins — How a cockpit remembers its speeds | In an MD-80 approach, the correspondence between airspeeds and wing configurations for the day's landing weight is computed once, 25 to 30 minutes before landing, by selecting a printed speed card with the displayed gross weight, and is stored in the positions of movable bugs on both airspeed indicators; when the plane slows 10 to 15 minutes later, the needle's approach to a bug cues each flap call by a judgment of spatial proximity. Hutchins argues that this memory belongs to the cockpit as a functional system and that speed bugs do not improve any pilot's memory but replace a recall-and-scale-reading task with a perceptual one. The account is a stylized description of mandated procedure, informed by more than 100 observer flights and simulator recordings, with no measured performance, no comparison of crews with and without bugs, and no failure cases; the claim that the arrangement changes what the system can do is established by analysis of the tasks, not by data. | Read |
| [NOTE-871](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-871.md) | Kirsh — The intelligent use of space | A classification, from video of cooks, assemblers and baggers, informal observation and the Tetris studies, of how people arrange things around them to cut the time and memory a task needs: arrangements that simplify choice (hide or highlight affordances, eliminate decisions, offload heuristic properties), arrangements that simplify perception (clustering, regions, marking, the vernier effect), and spatial dynamics that save internal computation (Tetris rotation, self-cueing). It frames the savings in search-complexity terms and links informational structuring to amortized computation in a footnote, but says the savings cannot in general be meaningfully quantified and offers no cost model, no measurements beyond the cited Tetris timings, and no case of an arrangement failing under a deadline. Its agents are experts arranging their own workspace in the medium and short term; long-term, pre-built environments are set aside. | Read |
| [NOTE-872](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-872.md) | Kirsh — Adapting the environment instead of oneself | A conceptual paper. It models a task as a directed graph of states and actions with a cost metric on transitions, and classifies how an agent can improve its payoff by actions external to the task: pruning hard initial states, routine maintenance, scouting ahead, tools (which change the graph), and actions that make a space more "cognitively congenial" (which leave the graph intact and reduce mental operations). It names amortization once, as a parenthetical gloss on chimps leaving nut-cracking stones in place, and gives an investment rule for maintenance (future benefit against present cost times an "interest factor" for risk) in words only. There is no cost model with reuse frequency, retrieval cost or staleness; mental cost lies outside the graph, and the paper says there is "no general theory" of congeniality. The empirical figures are unpublished pilot results. | Read |
| [NOTE-878](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-878.md) | Kirsh & Maglio — On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action | Kirsh and Maglio define an epistemic action as a physical action whose primary function is to reduce the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own mental computation, and argue from Tetris keystroke data that players rotate and translate pieces for that reason: zoids are rotated more than plan-then-act would need, rotation starts within a few hundred milliseconds of a zoid appearing, and a translate-to-wall check is used more the higher the drop. The computational saving is argued, not measured: physical rotation of 90° takes as little as 100 ms against an estimated 800–1200 ms mentally (a three-player pilot), and fewer attentional probes and less working memory are needed. The trade is physical action in place of internal computation at the moment of use, not precomputation or caching; the paper explicitly sets it against caching and chunking accounts of skill, and mentions amortized complexity only in passing for everyday cases such as sorting bolts before assembly. It says the choice fits a Stigler-style cost–benefit model in outline but that such models fail in detail, because an epistemic action's value depends on the particular internal computation it serves. | Read |
| [NOTE-883](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-883.md) | Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook & Rao — Deictic codes for the embodiment of cognition | At about a third of a second, the time scale of a saccade, the article models fixation as a pointer that binds a variable in a behavioural program to a place in the world, so that what is bound is only the task-relevant feature, fetched just before use. In a block-copying task subjects looked back at the model about 1.3 times per block on average, the commonest cycle being two looks per block (one apparently for colour, one for position), and chose this slowest, lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against about 1.5 s for copying from memory) though told to be fast; separating model and copy by 70° cut looks to 1.0 per block, and one-colour patterns that could be chunked cut them to 0.7. The authors read this as working memory having a "carrying cost" that exceeds the cost of re-acquiring from the world, but that cost is inferred from the choices and never measured or modelled, and the evidence is one task with small samples (seven subjects for the main data, three for the colour-change experiment) and no statistics reported in the article. What is left in the world is unprocessed input, not a computed result, and the article argues against precomputation where the needed products cannot be foreseen. | Read |
| [NOTE-887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-887.md) | Risko & Gilbert — Cognitive offloading | A short review that defines cognitive offloading as physical action that changes a task's information-processing requirements to reduce cognitive demand, splits it into offloading onto the body and into the world, and proposes a metacognitive model: whether people offload is a strategy choice driven by their evaluation of internal versus extended strategies, which tracks objective internal demand but can be wrong, and offloading in turn changes both memory and those evaluations. The evidence is a handful of choice/no-choice studies, summarised qualitatively; the review reports no effect sizes and no formal account of costs. It names costs (memory for offloaded content, GPS-impaired spatial memory, photo-taking impairment, automation complacency and bias, skill decay, inflated self-knowledge, a self-reinforcing drift toward external reliance). It does not frame offloading as computation reused over time, and says nothing about how often an offloaded result is used. | Read |
